entities.name: Prior work on metals and metal oxides established that water can dissociate directly on flat transition-metal surfaces via concerted chemisorption, that solvati
entities.description: Prior work on metals and metal oxides established that water can dissociate directly on flat transition-metal surfaces via concerted chemisorption, that solvation and undercoordinated sites such as corrugations/steps/kinks further enhance dissociation, and that on oxides such as rutile TiO2(110) oxygen vacancies promote heterolytic dissociation while pristine TiO2 can dissociate water through solvent-assisted proton-transfer pathways; similar proton-transfer behavior was also reported for solvated ZnO surfaces.
entities.evidence_span: On flat transition metals, water molecules can undergo direct dissociative chemisorption, colliding with the metal surface and cleaving an O-H bond to deposit H and OH fragments via a concerted mechanism.

evidence_spans: On flat transition metals, water molecules can undergo direct dissociative chemisorption, colliding with the metal surface and cleaving an O-H bond to deposit H and OH fragments via a concerted mechanism.
Solvation with other water molecules can facilitate this process.
When corrugations, steps, or kinks are introduced to the surface, metal-water dissociation can be further enhanced with binding to undercoordinated sites.

On metal oxide surfaces such as rutile TiO2(110), oxygen vacancies can help promote dissociation via heterolytic mechanisms in which a proton transfers to a neighboring surface oxygen, yielding two surface hydroxyls per defect.
in the case of pristine TiO2, water dissociation can proceed through solvent-assisted proton transfer pathways that vary from one-step to two-step processes depending on the facet.
Similar proton-transfer phenomena occur at solvated ZnO surfaces.

entities.name: Under solvation, two distinct reaction channels connect bare SV to chemisorbed products. One pathway forms an SV–H intermediate plus adjacent hydroxide by proto
entities.description: Under solvation, two distinct reaction channels connect bare SV to chemisorbed products. One pathway forms an SV–H intermediate plus adjacent hydroxide by proton abstraction; the other forms SV–OH while transferring a proton to the solvent via Grotthuss transport. Both have similar forward barriers (21.9 and 23.7 kcal/mol), both lower than the 28.4 kcal/mol gas-phase barrier, and the SV–OH/H3O+ intermediate is about 20 kcal/mol more stable. From either intermediate, the system proceeds to Hydroxy-SV and then SV-Ketone.
entities.evidence_span: The solvated free energy landscape is more intricate (see Figure 2c/d). Two distinct reaction channels now connect the bare SV to the chemisorbed products)

evidence_spans: The solvated free energy landscape is more intricate (see Figure 2c/d). Two distinct reaction channels now connect the bare SV to the chemisorbed products)
In the first pathway, the SV abstracts a proton from the nearby water to form an SV–H intermediate and an adjacent solvated hydroxide ion.
In the second, water attacks the vacancy oxygen-first to form SV–OH, transferring one of its protons to the surrounding media via the Grotthus mechanism.

Both processes occur with comparable forward free energy barriers – indicative of an early transition state governed primarily by O–H bond cleavage – but with the SV–OH/H3O+ intermediate being ∼20 kcal/mol more stable in free energy.
These forward barriers (21.9 kcal/mol for SV–H/OH– formation, and 23.7 kcal/mol for SV–OH/H3O+) are overall lower in free energy than for the concerted gas-phase process (28.4 kcal/mol).
From either intermediate, the system proceeds to the Hydroxy-SV and then to the SV-Ketone, which lies 74 kcal/mol below the solvated bare SV.

entities.name: Under solvation, two distinct reaction channels connect bare SV to chemisorbed products. One pathway forms an SV–H intermediate plus adjacent hydroxide by proton abstraction; the other forms SV–OH whi
entities.description: Under solvation, two distinct reaction channels connect bare SV to chemisorbed products. One pathway forms an SV–H intermediate plus adjacent hydroxide by proton abstraction; the other forms SV–OH while transferring a proton to the solvent via Grotthuss transport. Both have similar forward barriers (21.9 and 23.7 kcal/mol), both lower than the 28.4 kcal/mol gas-phase barrier, and the SV–OH/H3O+ intermediate is about 20 kcal/mol more stable. From either intermediate, the system proceeds to Hydroxy-SV and then SV-Ketone.
